deck: CS3307A OOD::Week 2::Interfaces vs Parameters vs Concretes

fields.Front: When should you use an interface, and what does it buy you?
fields.Back: When the variation is behavioral, i.e. different algorithms (console vs file logging; PayPal vs Stripe). It enables polymorphism and the Dependency Inversion Principle: consumers couple to the abstraction, not the concrete. Result: flexible, extensible, testable.

fields.Front: When should you use a parameter instead of subclasses?
fields.Back: When the variation is only data (numbers, labels, configuration values). Keep one class and configure it via constructor arguments or fields. This avoids subclass explosion for trivial differences and is lightweight and clear.

fields.Front: When is a plain concrete class with no abstraction acceptable, and what does it cost?
fields.Back: It is the smallest, simplest approach, fine for tiny apps or one-off utilities. The cost: consumers are tied to the concrete implementation, so it is harder to extend or swap behaviour later.

fields.Front: Case study 1: what is wrong with DebugLogger and ErrorLogger under ILogger?
fields.Back: They are identical except for the literal "[DEBUG] " versus "[ERROR] ": same algorithm (print to console), different data. The slide labels them 'pointless separate class'. With five log levels you would have five near-duplicate classes.

fields.Front: Case study 1: what is the right way to handle the logger level while keeping ILogger?
fields.Back: One parameterized concrete: class ConsoleLogger : public ILogger { std::string level; public: explicit ConsoleLogger(std::string lvl) : level(std::move(lvl)) {} void log(const std::string& msg) const override { std::cout << "[" << level << "] " << msg << "\n"; } }; Callers still hold ILogger&.

fields.Front: Read the signature virtual void log(const std::string& msg) const = 0;. What does each part mean?
fields.Back: const std::string&: pass by reference to avoid a copy, const because the message is not modified. Trailing const: the member function does not change the logger's state. = 0: pure virtual, so every implementation must provide log.

fields.Front: Case study 2: describe the design and state its trade-off.
fields.Back: A single concrete Logger with std::string level and no interface; log has no virtual and no override because there is nothing to override. Minimal and fine for tiny apps, but every caller names Logger, so wanting a different behaviour (file output) forces refactoring the callers.

fields.Front: Case study 3: what makes ConsoleLogger and FileLogger a legitimate use of an interface?
fields.Back: The variation is genuinely behavioural: ConsoleLogger prints [CONSOLE] to standard output while FileLogger opens its file in append mode (std::ofstream out(filename, std::ios::app)) and writes [FILE] there. Different algorithms, so separate classes under ILogger.

fields.Front: What role does AuditService play in case study 3, and what does its code look like?
fields.Back: It is the high-level consumer: class AuditService { ILogger& logger; public: explicit AuditService(ILogger& l) : logger(l) {} void record(const std::string& msg) { logger.log(msg); } }; It holds an injected ILogger& (aggregation) and calls log polymorphically, compiling without knowing FileLogger exists.

fields.Front: What does case study 3's main print or do?
fields.Back: AuditService a(console); a.record("User logged in."); prints [CONSOLE] User logged in.; AuditService b(file); b.record("Transaction completed."); appends [FILE] Transaction completed. to audit.log. The same AuditService class serves both.

fields.Front: Does FileLogger show that interfaces and parameters are mutually exclusive?
fields.Back: No, the opposite. FileLogger sits under the ILogger interface (behavioural variation) AND takes a data parameter, the filename, through explicit FileLogger(std::string fn). Use both mechanisms for the kind of variation each fits.

Supplying a class's dependencies from outside, usually through the constructor, rather than creating them inside. It is what turns pattern 1/3 into pattern 2/4, and what makes a class testable by letting a fake collaborator be substituted.

fields.Front: Structurally, what is case study 3 the same as?
fields.Back: Pattern 4, Abstract + Inject, applied to logging: AuditService/ILogger is the same shape as Checkout/IPaymentProcessor. Consumer holds a reference to the abstraction, concrete injected through the constructor.

fields.Text: Rule of thumb: behaviour differs -> {{c1::interface}}; only data differs -> {{c1::parameter}}; toy or simple case -> {{c1::concrete}}.

In explicit ConsoleLogger(std::string lvl) : level(std::move(lvl)) {}, explicit prevents {{c1::implicit conversion}} from a std::string to a ConsoleLogger, and std::move {{c1::moves the by-value parameter into the member instead of copying it}}.
fields.Extra: So ConsoleLogger x = "DEBUG"; is rejected. Use explicit on any single-argument constructor.

fields.Text: Case study summary: example 1 keeps the {{c1::abstraction}} but handles data-only variation with one parameterized class; example 2 has {{c1::no abstraction}} so callers depend on a concretion; example 3 uses {{c1::interfaces + DI}} because behaviour differs.
Interfaces suit {{c1::behavioral}} variation (different algorithms) and enable {{c1::polymorphism and DIP}}; parameters suit {{c1::data-only}} variation and avoid {{c1::subclass explosion}}.
Case study 1's lesson: when variation is only data such as label text, don't make {{c1::subclasses}}; keep the {{c1::interface}} and use {{c1::one parameterized class}}.
fields.Extra: DebugLogger and ErrorLogger are labelled 'pointless separate class' on the slide.

fields.Text: In case study 3, AuditService holds `{{c1::ILogger& logger}}` injected through its constructor ({{c1::aggregation}}) and record() makes a {{c1::polymorphic}} call to logger.log(msg).
